children.text: A shallow bay about
30–40 minutes

from Puerto Princesa city by car, where a popular day tour takes a bangka around small sandy islets such as Cowrie Island, Luli Island, and Starfish Island. The calm waves and short crossings make it especially good for family travelers with children.
Honda Bay is a wide bay on the Sulu Sea side, about
20km

northeast of Puerto Princesa city, Palawan's capital. Large and small islands, sandy islets, and coral reefs are scattered across the bay, mostly in shallow, calm water, so you can visit several islands with only short bangka rides. Being close to the city and easy to arrange, it has become, alongside the underground river tour, one of Puerto Princesa's signature day trips.

The bay's shore gives way to mangrove forests and fishing villages, and seagrass beds and coral reefs here and there serve as habitat for juvenile fish and starfish. The stars of a Honda Bay tour are the small islands. Well-equipped Cowrie Island has a beachfront restaurant, a bar, and rest areas, making it a good place to have lunch and relax. Luli Island, whose name means "island that sinks and rises," is mostly submerged at high tide and shows its sand at low tide, with good snorkeling around it. As its name suggests, Starfish Island has red and blue starfish scattered across the shallow seabed, which children especially love. In addition, privately owned Pandan Island is sometimes included in private tours.

Honda Bay tours run as a cooperative: the Honda Bay Boat Owners Association (HOBBAI) at Santa Lourdes pier assigns the bangkas and sets the fares. Fares per course are the same whichever bangka you board, so there is no haggling, and you usually pick either Course A (Pambato Reef, Luli Island, Cowrie Island) or Course B (Starfish Island, Luli Island, Cowrie Island). Although the bay has more than ten islands, only some are open to ordinary travelers. Snake Island, once famous for its long curving sandbar, was closed to protect the coral around
and is still not part of regular tours, and private islands such as Arreceffi Island, home to the Dos Palmas resort, are mostly for hotel guests. Tour boats start leaving around
and usually return around
2–3 PM
, and bangka service at the pier ends at

There are no grand limestone cliffs like El Nido or Coron, but the short crossings and gentle sea make it comfortable for weak swimmers, children, and older travelers alike. On one side of the bay there's also an island resort, Dos Palmas, where you can spend a quiet night.
It suits travelers who want to make the most of their first or last day in Palawan around a flight time, family travelers, and beginners at snorkeling.
Coral and tropical fish gather around this sandy islet, whose appearance changes with the tide. Visit at low tide to walk the exposed sandbar.
You can see starfish in knee-deep water. Don't lift them out of the water — they can't breathe out of it and will be harmed — so observe with your eyes only.
Eating a seafood lunch at tables in the shade of palm trees, then lying in a hammock, is the highlight of a Honda Bay tour. There's also a massage service and a bar.

A privately owned island with a white-sand beach and shade from palm trees, where you can enjoy seafood sold by fishermen and beach massages. It is not included in the standard Courses A and B, so you need to book a private tour or ask the boat owners association separately, and you should check the entrance fee and conditions of use with the island in advance.
In the open sea beyond Honda Bay, you can see dolphins and whale sharks from
April–October
, and whale sharks appear in especially large numbers in the week or so around the full moon. This is a dedicated tour separate from island hopping, leaving early around
and taking
6–8 hours
, and under the city tourism office's guidance it must be booked in advance through the boat owners association.
After finishing your Honda Bay tour, follow it up in the evening with a tour of the fireflies filling the mangrove trees along the Iwahig River south of the city, for a full day.
You can explore the Baywalk seaside promenade, the Immaculate Conception Cathedral, and Plaza Cuartel, a memorial to a World War II POW massacre, all on foot.

On a floating turtle-shaped "Sea School" platform, a boatman guide gives a short explanation of the coral reef ecology, and you snorkel on the surrounding reef. If you choose a course that includes Pambato Reef, the entrance fee is included in the bangka fare.

The bangka fare is per boat, not per person, so if you are traveling alone, a join tour that gathers 3–6 people is cheaper. With 4–6 people, renting directly works out cheaper per person.
Many direct flights connect Manila, Cebu, and Clark to Puerto Princesa International Airport (PPS). From Manila it takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
, at around
one way. The airport is in the city center, making transfers easy, and a Honda Bay tour is simple to fit in even with an early or late flight.
From Cebu (Mactan), Cebu Pacific and the PAL group operate direct flights daily, taking about
1 hour 20 minutes
, with one-way fares starting around

. From Clark, Cebu Pacific direct flights operate only on certain days of the week, so check the schedule before you leave. From Manila, Cebu Pacific, Philippine Airlines, and AirAsia fly several times a day, so it is easy to pick a time slot. Puerto Princesa airport is close to the city, so you can even fit a half-day tour into the afternoon you arrive.
The easiest way is a Honda Bay join tour through a city travel agency, including hotel round-trip pickup, bangka, lunch, snorkel gear, and some entrance fees, for about
per person. To go on your own, charter a tricycle from the city to Santa Lourdes pier for about
one way, about
30–40 minutes
, or take a jeepney and switch to a tricycle at the junction.
By public transport, take a Santa Lourdes-bound jeepney or multicab from the national highway in the city for about
per person; frequent stops mean it takes about
40–50 minutes
. The city tourism office advises chartering a tricycle from the city or the airport at
for 3 people, and details can be found at the
Puerto Princesa City Tourism Office Honda Bay guide
At the Santa Lourdes pier there is a bangka ticket office run by the Honda Bay Boat Owners Association formed by local boat owners, where you can rent a bangka directly. It costs about

per boat for 1–6 people, varying by course (including Pambato Reef or Starfish Island) and engine size, and from 7 people an additional fee is charged by headcount. Travel between islands is mostly within
10–20 minutes
. You pay the environmental fee at the pier, and a separate island entrance fee at each island.
Santa Lourdes pier operates from
. At the pier, you first pay the environmental fee of about
; the receipt is valid for about 6 months, so show it at other tourist sites in the city too. After paying the terminal fee of about
, you choose a course and engine (3-cylinder or 4-cylinder) at the boat owners association ticket office, and a bangka is assigned to you. Course A costs about
and Course B about
; if your group is larger than the 6-person capacity, about
extra applies for 7–10 people and about
extra for 11–15 people. There are no ATMs at the pier or on the islands, so you need cash.
November
through
May
is the dry season and good for visiting.
March
through
May

especially has the calmest sea and clearest water, the best conditions for snorkeling. Honda Bay faces the Sulu Sea on Palawan's east side, so it tends to stay calmer during the rainy season than the west coast, which takes the full force of the southwest monsoon.
From
June
to
October
is the rainy season, with frequent afternoon showers, and after heavy rain, river runoff can cloud the water. From
December
to
February

, the northeast monsoon Amihan brings windy days that can rock the bangka. Southern Palawan sees fewer direct typhoon hits than other parts of the Philippines, but a strong typhoon does pass through in some years, so check the forecast.

Snorkeling is best in the morning when the water is clearest, and the Luli Island sandbar is exposed much more widely if you time your visit to low tide. Puerto Princesa's monthly average temperature stays at
year-round with little variation;
January–April
is the driest peak season, and in
May
the daytime high climbs to about
, making it the hottest month. Rainfall is heaviest in
October
and typhoon risk is highest in
August–September
, so it is safer not to schedule sea trips then. In peak season join tours fill up early, so it is best to book a few days ahead.

Most people stay in Puerto Princesa city and visit as a day trip. City guesthouses and mid-range hotels run about
per night, and staying around Baywalk or Rizal Avenue is convenient for restaurants and shopping malls. Resort-style hotels with a pool and garden run about

per night. For a quiet island stay, you can choose an island resort inside Honda Bay, sold as a package with boat transport and meals for tens of thousands of pesos a night. There are also small beach resorts around Santa Lourdes pier and along the bay's shore.

Puerto Princesa is a city of fresh, affordable seafood. City seafood restaurants cook crab, shrimp, squid, and fish however you like, and some, such as the long-running KaLui with its traditional interior and seafood courses, are well known. Tamilok, a type of shipworm, skewered street snacks along Baywalk, and cool halo-halo are also worth trying. Island tour lunches often feature grilled fish, shrimp, pork barbecue, rice, and fruit. Palawan cashews and pearl accessories make popular souvenirs.

If you want to stay inside Honda Bay, Dos Palmas Island Resort & Spa on Arreceffi Island is the best-known choice. It is a private island resort with a beach, overwater villas, and a swimming pool; guests travel from the pier on the resort's own boat, so check the boat schedule when you book. On regular island tours, the buffet lunch on Cowrie Island costs about
, and on Starfish Island you can rent a shaded cottage to rest in for about
. Puerto Princesa strictly regulates single-use plastics (Ordinance No. 993), banning plastic bags, straws, and Styrofoam containers, so it helps to bring your own water bottle and shopping bag.
There are no ATMs at the pier or on the islands, so bring cash from the city. Small bills are handy for entrance fees and the environmental fee.
When booking a join tour, be sure to confirm whether entrance fees and the environmental fee are included, along with the list of islands visited. Cheaper tours often charge entrance fees separately.
If you charter a bangka yourself, checking the tide table and timing your visit to Luli Island and the sandbar islands at low tide gives much better scenery.
Snorkel gear is included in tours, but bringing your own mask is more hygienic and comfortable.
Some islands have little shade, so bring a hat, rash guard, and reef-safe sunscreen.
With the airport and pier both close by, it's possible to fit in a tour before an afternoon flight on your last day, but leave plenty of buffer between your tour return time and airport arrival.
Smart and Globe signals reach most islands, though they can be weak.
Tour boats usually all leave together around
8–9 AM
, crowding the first island, so if you charter your own bangka, it's best to leave around
or reverse the tour order.
Cowrie Island's restaurant runs short on seats at lunchtime in peak season, so if you're not on a join tour, it's best to order lunch as soon as you arrive.

The environmental fee is a common fee across Puerto Princesa city tourist sites, so if you have already paid it, for example on an underground river tour, you often do not need to pay again if you show the receipt. It is best to keep your receipt rather than throwing it away.
Lifting or touching starfish and coral out of the water is prohibited. Taking a starfish out for a photo threatens its life and must never be done.
Wear a life vest on the bangka, and never exceed the boat's capacity.
The shallow water has sea urchins and sharp coral, so wearing aqua shoes is a good idea.
The midday sun is strong and causes frequent sunburn, so take breaks in the shade often and drink plenty of water.
Entrance fee and environmental fee rules can change by decision of the city tourism office and the island management, so check the latest notices.
Many islands have no lifeguards on duty, so children must be watched by a guardian at their side at all times.
Bangka service at the pier ends at
and the wind picks up in the afternoon, making the waves higher, so avoid returning late in the afternoon, and on the day you fly, book a half-day course that finishes in the morning.
